name: Prostatic Adenocarcinoma, Gleason Scoring, and Prostatic Hyperplasia

reference.source: Sabiston Textbook of Surgery 22nd ed / Campbell-Walsh Urology 12th ed
clinicalPearls: BPH arises in the transition zone causing early obstruction; adenocarcinoma arises in the peripheral zone
Gleason Grade Group system (1 to 5) defines architectural differentiation and guides therapeutic decision-making
PSA velocity and free-to-total PSA ratio (< 15% suspicious) improve specificity over total PSA alone
Active surveillance is the standard of care for low-risk prostate cancer (Gleason 3+3=6, Grade Group 1)
Radical prostatectomy removes the prostate, seminal vesicles, and ampullae with pelvic lymphadenectomy
reference.pathophysiology: Prostatic adenocarcinoma develops primarily in peripheral zone acinar glands through progressive accumulation of genomic alterations including TMPRSS2-ERG gene fusions and PTEN tumor suppressor deletions. Androgens (dihydrotestosterone) driving androgen receptor signaling sustain tumor cell growth, with skeletal metastases classically producing dense osteoblastic bone remodeling.
additionalDifferentials: Benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH) with prominent nodular enlargement
Prostatic infarction with transient severe PSA elevation
additionalInvestigations: Serum total PSA, free-to-total PSA ratio, and PSA density
Multiparametric prostate MRI (mpMRI) with PI-RADS scoring
MRI-ultrasound targeted and systematic transperineal or transrectal core biopsy
Technetium-99m bone scintigraphy or PSMA PET-CT for metastatic staging
